<reason>Side B won by exposing a core contradiction in Side A's case and defending a realistic, tiered model of platform responsibility. Side A argued both that garments are forensically impossible for platforms to authenticate and that individual buyers are the "least-cost avoiders" who can verify items at home or hire third-party authenticators. Side B forced Side A to retreat to claiming buyers only perform a basic "sanity check," which left Side A unable to justify why platforms should keep their commissions when high-grade counterfeits fool buyers past brief dispute windows. Furthermore, Side B effectively dismantled Side A's warning that vintage markets would collapse by explaining that counterfeiters target recognizable, high-demand brands rather than obscure vintage pieces, allowing platforms to target physical checks where fraud clusters while absorbing refund risk and clawing back funds from scammers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's dismantling of Side A's "least-cost avoider" claim across [B2.1]-[B2.3], [B3.1]-[B3.2], and [B4.3]: Side B showed that if clothing authentication is too difficult for platforms at scale, individual buyers cannot possibly do it within three days, and forcing Side A to concede that buyers can only run a casual "sanity check" proved that buyers are unequipped to catch modern high-grade fakes.</best_rebuttal>
